description:
We are science, technology and music enthusiasts! Aspire to combine our data analysis knowledge with music theory specialty to create scientific art. After all, art and science are both art, aren’t they?

Our team includes physicists, data analysts, musicians and people who do both :)
summary: We have created a demo that translates videos of global precipitation data into both appealing and scientifically informative music. By tracking the location of storms, their rotation, velocity and size we create music that differs in pitch, vibrato, timbre and the distribution of sound between the ears. Our goal is to make data and the beauty of our world accessible to the blind and visually impaired, in a way that helps them to intuitively perceive the image in their minds.
details:
We have joined the NASA Space Apps challenge to make science and the beauty of our world accessible for everyone. In 2026 still most of the scientific data is visual, which renders it inaccessible for the blind and visually impaired. Therefore there is a social impact in making this data accessible in another way - in our case - via sound. It is also beneficial for scientists in general to explore their data in a different modality, and by that maybe being inspired with new research questions and conclusions. 

In our project, we have decided to focus on global precipitation data, provided by the EIC. Although different sonifications already exist out there, our project is unique since it analyzes videos and not just frozen frames. We are able to track rain clouds both in space and time. What is also important to note is that in contrast to other sonifications, we have made the music generated by the data both musically appealing and scientifically informative. In other words, when a visually impaired person uses our demo, he or she can actually understand in real time, while listening, what is happening to the storm.

In order to do that, we have mapped the screen to audio - moving the mouse horizontally changes how the sound is split between the right and left headphones. Moving the mouse up or down, changes the pitch. All that is necessary for the first step - the users choose themselves, by audio, the storms that they want to focus on and translate into music. When they pass a storm with their mouse, rain or snow sounds are played. That way, they can click and choose a certain storm to follow, while knowing intuitively where it is on the screen.

When pressing "play", using the spacebar, the music starts. Our algorithm follows the selected storms, and translates them into music regarding a few parameters:

1. Movement on the X-axis changes the distribution of the sound between the ears - storms that occur on the right side of the map, for example, will correlate to sound sent to the right ear. That is, of course, dynamic, according to the movement of the clouds.

2. Movement along the Y-axis correlates to the pitch of the sound.

3. Storms' rotation is translated into vibrato. The faster the rotation is, the faster the vibrato.

4. When the storm changes its size and becomes bigger or smaller - the timbre changes.

It is possible to choose just one storm, or multiple storms to follow. If the user is interested in getting more information about the translation of the data - pressing ctrl+i opens an audio explanation.

The software tools we used include: Copilot, Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, VSCode, Logic Pro X, GitHub and Git. The coding languages we used are JavaScript, Python, CSS, HTML and Shell.

Code: https://github.com/itaynn/Gravitunes
